query: For high-entropy alloys intended for demanding engineering applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs the retention or loss of toughness, and why? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, the predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In FCC high‐entropy alloys, surface oxidation induced by a high-temperature/pressure water environment suppresses the nucleation of Shockley partial dislocations, thereby preventing the formation of ductile HCP phases and instead favoring the formation of a more brittle BCC phase. This change in deformation mechanism governs the loss of toughness compared to a vacuum environment.
generation.material_initial_state: A clean-surfaced, single-phase FCC high-entropy alloy (e.g., Fe40Ni40Cr20 or equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi) prepared in an unoxidized state.
generation.intervention: Perform atomistic uniaxial tensile simulations under two controlled environmental conditions: one in vacuum and the other in a simulated high-temperature/pressure water environment that induces surface oxidation.
generation.conditions: Simulations maintained at identical strain rates and temperatures with the only variable being the ambient environment (vacuum versus oxidizing high-temperature/pressure water).
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of an oxide layer on the alloy surface in the water environment.
generation.mechanism: In vacuum, tensile deformation promotes the generation of Shockley partial dislocations from surfaces and grain boundaries, which enables an FCC-to-HCP phase transition associated with higher ductility and toughness. However, in the corrosive water environment, the oxide layer suppresses these dislocation events, leading instead to an FCC-to-BCC phase transition, which results in reduced ductility and overall toughness.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under vacuum conditions, the alloy will develop an HCP phase from Shockley partial nucleation, retaining higher toughness. In contrast, under high-temperature/pressure water conditions, the oxidized surface will inhibit Shockley partials, leading to a preferential formation of a brittle BCC phase and a measurable reduction in ductility and toughness relative to the vacuum baseline.
generation.baseline: Vacuum tensile simulations where the pristine alloy exhibits Shockley partial dislocation formation and consequent HCP phase development that supports toughness retention.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis should hold for FCC-structured high-entropy alloys with relatively low stacking fault energies in environments where surface oxidation can occur (i.e., high-temperature and high-pressure water) and under strain rates typical of atomistic simulations.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the toughness reduction and the phase fraction shifts may vary with alloy composition, oxidation kinetics, and simulation parameters. Detailed quantitative outcomes remain uncertain until experimentally or computationally determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct atomistic uniaxial tensile simulations on an FCC high-entropy alloy sample in two scenarios: one under vacuum and one under high-temperature/pressure water conditions. Monitor the nucleation of Shockley partial dislocations, track phase transitions (quantifying HCP versus BCC phase fractions), and generate stress-strain curves to evaluate ductility and toughness.
measurements: Phase fraction analysis: Quantify the relative amounts of FCC, HCP, and BCC phases post-deformation.
Dislocation activity: Record frequency and mode (Shockley partials vs. other types) of dislocation nucleation.
Mechanical properties: Measure tensile strength, ductility, and toughness from stress-strain data.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if, in the high-temperature/pressure water simulation, the suppression of Shockley partial dislocation nucleation is not observed and the phase evolution mirrors that in the vacuum simulation (i.e., similar levels of HCP formation without a concomitant increase in BCC phase or reduction in ductility).

cited_evidence.text: AbstractHigh entropy alloys (HEAs) have demonstrated excellent potential in various applications owing to the unique properties. One of the most critical issues of HEAs is the stress corrosion cracking (SCC) which limits its reliability in practical applications. However, the SCC mechanisms have not been fully understood yet because of the difficulty of experimental measuring of atomic-scale deformation mechanisms and surface reactions. In this work, we conduct atomistic uniaxial tensile simulations using an FCC-type Fe40Ni40Cr20 alloy as a typical simplification of normal HEAs, in order to reveal how a corrosive environment such as high-temperature/pressure water affects the tensile behaviors and deformation mechanisms. In a vacuum, we observe the generation of layered HCP phases in an FCC matrix during tensile simulation induced by the formation of Shockley partial dislocations from surface and grain boundaries. In this work, uniaxial tensile simulations of FCC-type Fe40Ni40Cr20 alloy (as a simplified model of HEAs) are conducted in vacuum and high-temperature/pressure water environment to clarify the effect of corrosive environment on the deformation mechanisms. In vacuum, layered HCP phases are formed from FCC matrix during tensile simulation due to the generation of Shockley partial dislocations from surface and grain boundary. While, in the corrosive water environment, alloy surface is oxidized by the reactions with water and this oxidized surface layer can suppress the generation of Shockley partial dislocation as well as the resulted FCC-to-HCP phase transition; instead, generation of BCC phase is preferred to release the tensile stress and stored elastic energy, leading to an enhanced elastic modulus and reduced ductility. Thus, we revealed that the deformation mechanism of Fe40Ni40Cr20 alloy is changed by the presence of high-temperature/pressure water environment—from FCC-to-HCP phase transition in vacuum to FCC-to-BCC phase transition in water. This study as a theoretical fundamental may contribute to the further improvement of HEAs with high resistance to SCC in experiments.

reading.lever: Switch environmental conditions (vacuum vs. high-temperature/pressure water) in atomistic tensile simulations.
reading.why: This approach directly isolates the effect of surface oxidation on dislocation activity and phase transitions, providing clear insights into the toughness retention mechanism in HEAs.
